newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends little changed to firmer in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends little changed to firmer in U.S..

text.p: The dollar closed little changed against the mark and barely firmer versus the yen amid position squaring before European finance ministers convene in Dublin and the Federal Reserve meets on Tuesday, experts said. The Dublin talks, which start in earnest on Saturday, are seen as key for keeping considerable political momentum behind launching a single European currency in January 1999.

"As time goes on, it seems like the countries, France and Germany, seem to be determined to try and get their budgetary matters in accord with Maastricht targets," said Tom Benfer, director, foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.
"So, people feel the (European) convergence is going to happen eventually," Benfer said. "So, that's why the mark was sold off in overnight trading."
The French franc had soared to a two-month high against the mark on Friday, but the German unit managed to cut its losses against the franc and other currencies including the dollar in New York.
The dollar finished at 1.5151/59 marks, a tad lower than 1.5160/65 at the open. The U.S. currency closed at 109.92/99 yen, up from 109.80/85 yen.
Speculation about whether the Fed will hike interest rates on Tuesday to head off any inflationary pressures has preoccupied the foreign exchange market.

Early in the week, news that eight out of 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System had requested an increase in the five percent discount rate heightened expectations that the central bank may in fact decide to push up rates.
By Friday, currency traders had largely priced into dollar exchange rates the possibility that the Fed may increase rates by 25 basis points, traders said.

In light of this view, there was some reluctance to short dollars and a preference to be long dollars before the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the Fed's policy-setting panel, gathers on Tuesday.
"Given the Dublin meeting and given the FOMC meeting on Tuesday, it's difficult to find a reason to be short dollars," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
"Off of both of those, you would have a tendency to be longs dollars and that's the way the market is currently setting up," he added.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.2386/94 Swiss francs, down from 1.2420/27 at the opening.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3670/75 from C$1.3690/95.
